Is Every Trapezoid a Parallelogram?

GeometryTrianglesParadoxes
Game: This is a picture, not a game: drag the corners of a trapezoid and see which lengths really match.
How to play: Drag A, B, C or D, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show names, equal lengths, the claim or a hint.
Look for the math

An argument looks like a proof that every trapezoid is a parallelogram. Move the corners: the two marked pieces of the diagonal stay the same length even when the two bases are very different. Where did the proof go wrong?

The step that cheats

Write the top base AD = a, the bottom base BC = b, and the pieces of the diagonal x = AG, y = GH, z = CH. The page's two similar-triangle proportions give x = (a/b)(y + z) and z = (a/b)(x + y). Subtracting them gives z - x = (a/b)(x - z). Dividing by z - x would give a/b = -1, and taking absolute values would force a = b. But that division is division by zero: the honest conclusion is z - x = 0, so x = z.

What is really equal

Adding the equal lengths makes two parallelograms: AFBC and ACED. Hence BF is parallel and equal to AC. Two pairs of similar triangles then give the page's formulas (3) and (4): x / BF = a / (a + b) and z / BF = a / (a + b). So AG = CH whatever the base lengths; the logic test confirms this and both formulas for 2,768 trapezoids, along with CG / AG = AH / CH = b / a.

The algebra agrees

Formulas (1) and (2) also imply (x + y)/z = (z + y)/x, or x² + xy = z² + zy. With f(w) = w² + wy, this says f(x) = f(z). That parabola has its lowest point at (-y/2, -y²/4) and is strictly increasing for w > -y/2, so two positive values with y > 0 cannot give the same answer unless they are equal. One detail the page leaves out: when the top base is longer than the bottom one, G and H swap places along AC, so y = GH becomes negative and that last monotonicity step needs the pictured order (bottom base longer). With GH signed along the diagonal, formulas (1) and (2) hold in both orders and x = z always does.

So is every trapezoid one?

No. One common definition of a trapezoid requires its two parallel sides to be unequal; the starting picture here has a about 56 and b about 133, yet AG = CH. The two marks mean the diagonal is cut in equal end pieces, not that the bases are equal. Test the "Claim" box to see those two pieces marked on the starting shape.

Try this: drag A to the right until AD is longer than BC. The marks on AG and CH still match; only the order of G and H along the diagonal changes.
